quote: Now the only requirement is that you have a credit score above 670. Is that true for you?
stewart_read: When the customer pushes back on why credit matters, the rep admits 'I honestly don't know. I'm kind of on the bottom of the food chain here' rather than giving the escape-hatch redirect to the specialist.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep's honesty could be read as transparency-building rather than a gap, since the customer had excellent credit and moved on without friction.
coaching_implication: Coach the universal escape hatch ('that's exactly what our specialist will walk you through') instead of self-deprecating uncertainty — the current phrasing undercuts the rep's authority even when it doesn't cost the deal.

quote: Yeah. So the the way the program works, there's no upfront cost, and you don't have to pay for install.
stewart_read: Customer's direct cost question is answered with a full financial-mechanism explanation (bill swap, inflation, install costs) instead of the redirect-to-design canonical response.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: rep may be trying to defuse concern before it becomes a hard objection later. But the explanation itself creates the confusion seen next at 03:55, undermining that read.
coaching_implication: Use rebuttals.price_estimate_before_design's canonical redirect: acknowledge the question is fair, then pivot to needing bill info for real numbers, rather than explaining the payment mechanism in the abstract.

stewart_read: The customer explicitly states the mechanism explanation didn't land — direct evidence that over-explaining backfired into confusion rather than curiosity.
coaching_implication: This is the moment to replay with the rep: the fix isn't a better explanation, it's not explaining — pivot straight to 'let's look at your bill and I'll show you the real numbers' instead of narrating the swap mechanism a second time.

quote: I actually got two electric bills. I got a I got a pool house for my swimming pool too.
stewart_read: A second electric meter for a pool house is a higher-usage-profile signal (additional load) that could support a larger system size or be framed as extra savings potential, but the rep treats it purely as a data-collection complication.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep was mid bill-collection logistics and reasonably kept focus narrow on the primary meter given the customer volunteered the pool bill is only ~$30/month, making it low-value to dwell on.
coaching_implication: Even when low-dollar, a second meter is worth a one-line acknowledgment ('good to know, that's extra usage we can factor in') so the design conversation later doesn't feel like a surprise when it surfaces again with the closer.

quote: What? The that's on me to show up or what?
stewart_read: Customer reacts with alarm to the idea of an in-person visit; rep does not name why the default is in-person (design walkthrough value) before offering the phone alternative, so the concession looks reactive rather than framed as a choice.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: rep may have simply matched the customer's clear preference efficiently rather than defending the in-person format, which is a reasonable move for an older, cautious customer.
coaching_implication: When a customer balks at in-person, briefly note the value of the in-person visual before offering phone as an equally valid option — this avoids the sense that phone is a downgrade or that the rep caved.

quote: I don't know if I'm comfortable with it.
stewart_read: Customer states discomfort directly; rep's response is a same-breath channel swap ('We could always do a phone call') without acknowledging the discomfort itself.
alternative_hypothesis: The discomfort was resolved in the customer's very next line once the phone option was offered, and the customer volunteered his age (73) and cash-pay preference unprompted immediately after — suggesting the practical fix (phone option) addressed the actual concern (a stranger coming to the house) rather than requiring a verbal empathy beat. This is a low-urgency, quickly self-resolved moment, not a significant miss.
coaching_implication: Minor: a brief one-line acknowledgment ('totally understand, no problem at all') before pivoting to the phone option would cost nothing and land marginally warmer, but this did not cost the call — flag as a light touch-up, not a priority coaching item.

quote: So I'd like to know Cox. I need to know Cox and all that. It's worth well, I'm 73 years old. So if I gotta put a bunch of money in it, then it wasn't worth it to me to say so.
stewart_read: A 73-year-old customer stating he doesn't want to sink money into something at his age is a classic cost/worth-it objection; rep responds only with 'you don't have to put any money into it,' a factual reassurance rather than a flip that reframes his current bill as the ongoing cost he's already sinking money into.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read is well-supported here — the rep had the customer's own $200+/month bill figure in hand from 01:27 and did not use it, a clean missed flip rather than a deliberate deferral.
coaching_implication: Coach the flip: 'What's not worth it is the $200+ a month you're already sending to C&T with nothing to show for it' — using his own bill number turns his age-based hesitation into a reason to act now rather than wait.

quote: not a problem. I pay cash for my cars and everything.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers an explicit cash-pay financing preference unprompted — a stable operational fact about how he intends to transact, distinct from his age/anxiety framing.
coaching_implication: Flag this for the closer directly: customer prefers cash purchase over financing, which should shape which program options the specialist leads with.
